title: An exploration of dataset bias in single-step retrosynthesis prediction
experiments_summary: The study generated a retrosynthesis-specific dataset called USPTO-retro (1,103,781 atom-mapped reaction SMILES) from the USPTO reaction database using a standardized preprocessing pipeline that removes reagents and erroneous reactions. Reaction templates were extracted using the LocalTemplate algorithm, yielding 10,028 local reaction templates. The dataset was split into training, validation, and test sets using a random 90:5:5 split (full split), with reactions sharing the same product assigned to the same subset to prevent data leakage. Two additional splitting strategies were applied to 10%, 25%, and 50% subsets of the training data: (1) a narrow split, which sequentially increases the number of unique reaction templates across subsets while filtering validation and test sets to only include seen templates, and (2) a broad split, which randomly samples fractions of reactions across all templates while keeping validation and test sets unchanged. Three state-of-the-art single-step retrosynthesis models were trained on these splits: LocalRetro (template-based), MEGAN (graph-based template-free), and RootAligned (SMILES-based template-free), each using their respective repositories with default hyperparameters; RootAligned models on the broad split used a separately optimized hyperparameter set. All models were evaluated using the Syntheseus platform, which filters invalid and duplicate predictions. Evaluation metrics included top-k accuracy (proportion of test reactions where ground truth reactants appear in top-k predictions, with top-10 as the primary metric) and top-k round-trip accuracy (proportion of top-k predicted reactants that regenerate the original product via a forward reaction model, reported at top-1 and top-5). The forward model used for round-trip evaluation was RootAligned trained on the full USPTO-retro training set. Template frequency bias was analyzed by computing top-10 accuracy stratified by template frequency bins across all models. Tanimoto similarity between training and test set products was calculated using Morgan fingerprints with RDKit, with a similarity threshold of 0.4. Two external test sets were created from the commercial Pistachio database after filtering for non-overlap with USPTO-retro training data: Pistachio ID (10,000 reactions with in-distribution templates) and Pistachio OOD (10,000 reactions with unseen, out-of-distribution templates). The broad split experiments were used to evaluate generalization to novel products (Pistachio ID), and the narrow split experiments were used to evaluate generalization to novel disconnections (Pistachio OOD). Template oversampling and undersampling behavior of LocalRetro was analyzed by examining the ranked list of predicted templates relative to the true test distribution.
